On 4 September 476, a Germanic military commander named Odoacer removed the young emperor Romulus Augustulus from his throne in Ravenna, Italy. Odoacer did not take the title of emperor himself. Instead he sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople. Historians often use this moment to mark the end of the Western Roman Empire.

At its height in the second century CE, the Roman Empire stretched from Britain to Egypt and from Spain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps 60 million people. Its roads, laws, cities, aqueducts and Latin language shaped Europe, North Africa and the Middle East.

Rome's decline was long and had many causes. Civil wars between generals, economic troubles, plague, and the cost of defending enormous borders weakened the state. In 395 the empire was divided permanently into eastern and western halves.

From the late fourth century, groups such as the Goths, Vandals and Franks moved into Roman lands, sometimes as allies and soldiers, sometimes as invaders. Rome itself was sacked by the Visigoths in 410 and by the Vandals in 455. The Vandals also took the rich province of North Africa, around Carthage.

By 476 the western emperor controlled little more than Italy. Odoacer's act was quiet, almost symbolic.

The Eastern Roman Empire, which historians call the Byzantine Empire, continued for nearly a thousand years more, until Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453. And Roman influence never really ended: Latin grew into Italian, Spanish, French, Portuguese and Romanian, and Roman law still underlies many legal systems.

en.title: The Hijra: the Prophet Muhammad moves to Medina
en.text:
In 622 CE, the Prophet Muhammad and his followers left Mecca and moved to the oasis town of Yathrib, about 450 kilometres to the north. The town became known as Medina, the City of the Prophet. This journey, the Hijra, or migration, marks the beginning of the Islamic calendar.

Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 into the Quraysh tribe. Mecca was a trading town and the site of the Kaaba, a shrine visited by pilgrims. According to Islamic tradition, around 610 he began receiving revelations from God through the angel Jibril (Gabriel), which were later collected as the Quran.

He preached that there is one God, and called for justice, care for the poor, orphans and widows, and moral responsibility. His message won followers, but many powerful Meccans opposed it because it challenged their religion and their trade in pilgrims. Muslims faced pressure and persecution, and some early Muslims took refuge in the Christian kingdom of Aksum in Ethiopia.

In Medina, Muhammad became both religious and political leader. He set out an agreement, often called the Constitution of Medina, for the town's communities, including Jewish tribes. The first mosque was built there.

After years of conflict, Mecca came under Muslim control in 630. Muhammad died in Medina in 632.

Within a century, Islam spread from Spain to Central Asia. It later travelled along trade routes to West Africa, the Swahili coast and Southeast Asia, shaping language, architecture, law and learning. Today about a quarter of the world's people are Muslim, and the Islamic year is still counted from the Hijra.

en.title: The oldest dated printed book
en.text:
A copy of a Buddhist scripture called the Diamond Sutra, printed in China, carries a note at its end giving a date that corresponds to 11 May 868 CE. It is the oldest surviving printed book with a clear date, nearly 600 years before Gutenberg's Bible.

The book is a scroll about five metres long, made of sheets of paper pasted together. It was printed with carved wooden blocks: each whole page was cut in reverse into a block of wood, inked, and pressed onto paper. The opening picture shows the Buddha preaching to his disciple Subhuti, a finely detailed woodcut.

The note at the end says that a man named Wang Jie had the book made for free distribution, on behalf of his two parents. Printing scriptures to share was believed to bring spiritual merit.

The scroll was found in 1900 in a sealed cave library at Dunhuang, an oasis town on the Silk Road. The library had been closed up around the year 1000 and held tens of thousands of manuscripts in many languages. In 1907 the explorer Aurel Stein took the scroll to Britain; it is now in the British Library, a fact that remains controversial.

China also invented paper, around the second century CE or earlier, and later movable type. Papermaking spread along the Silk Road to the Islamic world, where Baghdad had paper mills by the late eighth century, and from there to Europe.

The Diamond Sutra reminds us that printing has a long, global history, and that East Asia led the way.

en.title: Genghis Khan unites the Mongols
en.text:
In 1206, at a great assembly called a kurultai near the Onon River, the chiefs of the Mongol tribes proclaimed a leader named Temüjin as their ruler. He took the title Genghis Khan, often understood as "universal ruler". Within 70 years, his family would rule the largest connected land empire in history.

Temüjin was born around 1162. His father was poisoned when he was a boy, and his family was abandoned by their clan, surviving by hunting and gathering. Through courage, loyal friendships and alliances, he rose to unite the feuding tribes of the steppe.

He reorganised Mongol society into military units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand, mixing tribes to break old loyalties, and promoted people for ability rather than birth. Mongol horsemen were superb archers, moving faster than any army of the time, with several horses per rider.

The Mongols conquered northern China, Central Asia, Persia and Russia, and later reached Eastern Europe and the Middle East. Cities that resisted, such as Merv, Nishapur and Baghdad in 1258, were destroyed with enormous loss of life. Millions died in the conquests.

Yet the empire also connected the world. Under Mongol rule, often called the Pax Mongolica, the Silk Roads were safer for merchants and travellers, including Marco Polo. Ideas, technologies and religions moved between China, Persia and Europe. The Mongols allowed freedom of religion and created a fast relay postal system.

Genghis Khan died in 1227. His grandson Kublai Khan conquered all of China and founded the Yuan dynasty. In Mongolia, Genghis Khan is honoured as the father of the nation.

en.title: Magna Carta is sealed
en.text:
On 15 June 1215, in a meadow called Runnymede beside the River Thames, King John of England set his seal on a document demanded by his rebellious barons. It became known as Magna Carta, the Great Charter.

King John was deeply unpopular. He had lost English lands in France, raised heavy taxes to pay for wars, and punished nobles without fair trial. In 1215 a group of barons rebelled and captured London.

Magna Carta was a peace treaty. Most of its 63 clauses dealt with the barons' specific complaints about inheritance, taxes, forests and debts. But a few clauses had a much bigger future. One said that no free man could be imprisoned, stripped of his rights or property, or punished except by the lawful judgement of his peers or by the law of the land. Another said that justice would not be sold, denied or delayed.

The charter failed at first. Within weeks the Pope annulled it at John's request and civil war broke out. But after John died in 1216, the charter was reissued several times in revised form, and in 1225 it became part of English law.

Over the centuries Magna Carta grew into a symbol of the idea that rulers are subject to the law. It influenced the English Bill of Rights in 1689, the United States Constitution and Bill of Rights, and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948.

At the time it protected only a small group of powerful men. Its later fame came from people who used its words to demand rights for everyone.

en.title: Great Zimbabwe at its height
en.text:
Around 1300, on a granite hilltop and the valley below in today's southern Zimbabwe, stood the largest stone city in sub-Saharan Africa. Its great walls were built from thousands of granite blocks fitted together without any mortar. Its name, Great Zimbabwe, comes from the Shona words for "houses of stone".

Great Zimbabwe was built by the ancestors of the Shona people between the eleventh and fifteenth centuries. At its height it may have been home to around 10,000 to 18,000 people. The Hill Complex was probably the home of the king and a religious centre. Below it, the Great Enclosure has an outer wall about 11 metres high and 250 metres long, with a mysterious solid conical tower inside.

The city's wealth came from cattle and from trade. Gold mined on the Zimbabwe plateau was carried to the coast at Sofala and sold to Swahili merchants of Kilwa, who shipped it across the Indian Ocean. Archaeologists at Great Zimbabwe have found glass beads from India, pottery from Persia and porcelain from China.

Eight carved soapstone birds were found at the site, probably symbols of royal ancestors. One of them is now on Zimbabwe's flag and coat of arms.

When European colonists arrived in the nineteenth century, many refused to believe Africans had built Great Zimbabwe, inventing theories about foreign builders. Archaeology proved them wrong, and the colonial government tried to suppress the truth.

When Rhodesia won independence in 1980, the new nation took the name Zimbabwe in honour of this city. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

en.title: The Black Death reaches Europe
en.text:
In October 1347, trading ships from the Black Sea docked at Messina in Sicily. Sailors on board were sick and dying. They had brought the bubonic plague, and within four years the disease known as the Black Death killed perhaps a third to a half of Europe's population.

The plague is caused by a bacterium, Yersinia pestis, carried by fleas that live on rats and other rodents. It probably began in Central Asia and spread along the trade routes of the Mongol world. In 1346 it reached Caffa, a trading port in Crimea, from where Italian ships carried it into the Mediterranean.

Victims developed painful swellings called buboes in the groin, armpits and neck, along with fever. Many died within days. A form that spread through the lungs could kill even faster.

The plague struck the Middle East and North Africa too. Cairo, one of the world's largest cities, lost a huge part of its people.

No one at the time understood the cause. Some blamed bad air, the stars or God's anger. Groups called flagellants whipped themselves in public. Terribly, many Jewish communities were falsely blamed for poisoning wells and were massacred.

The Black Death changed society. With so many workers dead, survivors could demand higher wages, weakening the old feudal system. Cities created health boards, and Venice began isolating ships for 40 days, quaranta giorni, which gave us the word quarantine.

Plague returned many times over the following centuries. Today it is treatable with antibiotics, but the Black Death remains one of the deadliest pandemics in human history.

en.title: Admiral Zheng He's treasure fleet sets sail
en.place: Nanjing, China, to the Indian Ocean
en.text:
In 1405, the first of seven great voyages left China under the command of Admiral Zheng He. His fleet of treasure ships was the largest the world had ever seen, and over the next 28 years it sailed as far as Arabia and the coast of East Africa.

Zheng He was born around 1371 in Yunnan into a Muslim family. Captured as a boy by Ming armies, he became a court official and a trusted ally of the Yongle Emperor, who sent him to show China's power and wealth to the lands of the Indian Ocean.

The first fleet is said to have had more than 300 ships and nearly 28,000 people. The largest ships were described as many times larger than the ships of Columbus. Historians debate their exact size, but they were certainly enormous.

The fleets visited Southeast Asia, India, Sri Lanka, Hormuz in Persia, Arabia and the Swahili coast, including Mogadishu, Brava and Malindi. They brought silk, porcelain and gifts, and returned with spices, precious stones, ambassadors, and exotic animals. Malindi's envoys sent a giraffe to China, where it was celebrated as a qilin, a mythical creature of good fortune.

These were not voyages of conquest like the later European expeditions, but they did use force when challenged.

After the Yongle Emperor died, the Ming court turned inward. The voyages ended after 1433, records were reportedly destroyed, and building large ocean-going ships was restricted. Fragments of Chinese porcelain are still found along the East African coast, and legends in Kenya tell of shipwrecked Chinese sailors who stayed.

en.title: Oba Ewuare the Great rebuilds Benin
en.text:
Around 1440, a ruler named Ewuare became Oba, or king, of Benin, in the forests of what is now southern Nigeria. Remembered as Ewuare the Great, he turned the kingdom into a powerful empire and rebuilt its capital, Benin City, into one of the most impressive cities in Africa.

Ewuare strengthened the power of the Oba, created new councils of chiefs, and expanded the kingdom through war. He rebuilt Benin City with broad, straight streets and enormous earthworks. The walls and moats of Benin, built over centuries, may have stretched thousands of kilometres in total, one of the largest earthworks ever created before modern machines.

The court supported guilds of craftsmen. Bronze-casters, ivory carvers and wood carvers worked only for the Oba. Using the lost-wax method, they made thousands of brass plaques, heads and figures, recording kings, warriors, ceremonies and visitors. Together these are known as the Benin Bronzes.

Portuguese visitors arrived in the 1480s and described a large, well-ordered city. Benin traded pepper, cloth and ivory with Europeans, and later was drawn into the Atlantic slave trade.

In 1897, a British force attacked Benin City, burned it and looted thousands of the bronzes and ivories, which were sold and scattered to museums around the world. The Oba was exiled.

The kingdom of Benin and its Oba still exist today within Nigeria. In recent years, museums in Germany, Britain and elsewhere have begun returning Benin Bronzes, a long-awaited step toward repairing that historic theft.

en.title: The Maya city of Tikal at its height
en.text:
Around 700 CE, the city of Tikal, deep in the rainforests of today's Guatemala, was one of the greatest cities of the Maya world. Stone temple-pyramids rose above the trees, some more than 60 metres high, and tens of thousands of people lived in and around the city.

The Maya civilisation spread across southern Mexico, Guatemala, Belize and Honduras. Its Classic period, roughly 250 to 900 CE, was a time of many competing city-states, each ruled by a divine king, called k'uhul ajaw.

The Maya were remarkable scholars. They developed the most complete writing system of the ancient Americas, combining signs for words and syllables, carved on monuments and painted in folding books made of bark paper. They used the concept of zero and a counting system based on twenty. Their astronomers tracked the movements of the Sun, Moon and Venus with great precision, and their Long Count calendar recorded dates over thousands of years.

Tikal had a long rivalry with the city of Calakmul. Inscriptions record wars, alliances and captured kings. In 695, Tikal's king Jasaw Chan K'awiil defeated Calakmul, and he was buried in the famous Temple I.

Recent laser surveys from the air, called LiDAR, have revealed that the Maya lowlands held far more people than once thought, with roads, farms and defences hidden under the forest.

In the ninth century many southern Maya cities were abandoned, probably because of drought, warfare and environmental stress. But the Maya did not disappear. Millions of Maya people live in the region today and speak around 30 Maya languages.

en.title: Columbus reaches the Caribbean
en.text:
On 12 October 1492, after more than two months at sea, three Spanish ships commanded by the Genoese navigator Christopher Columbus reached an island in the Bahamas. Its Taíno inhabitants called it Guanahani. Columbus named it San Salvador and claimed it for the Spanish crown.

Columbus believed he could reach Asia by sailing west. He greatly underestimated the size of the Earth and had no idea that two continents lay in the way. Funded by Queen Isabella and King Ferdinand of Spain, he left with the Niña, the Pinta and the Santa María. Until his death he insisted he had reached the edge of Asia, which is why the islands were called the West Indies and their people "Indians".

The Americas were not empty or unknown. Tens of millions of people lived there, in societies ranging from small villages to the vast empires of the Aztecs and Incas. Norse sailors had also reached Newfoundland around the year 1000.

What followed was one of the biggest turning points in world history, often called the Columbian Exchange. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava and cocoa travelled to Europe, Africa and Asia. Horses, cattle, wheat and sugar cane went west.

But diseases brought by Europeans, such as smallpox and measles, killed a huge share of Indigenous peoples, who had no immunity. Conquest, enslavement and forced labour destroyed many societies. To replace Indigenous workers, Europeans began transporting enslaved Africans across the Atlantic in enormous numbers.

For this reason, 12 October is marked very differently today: as Columbus Day in some places, and as Indigenous Peoples' Day or a day of resistance in others.

en.title: The fall of Tenochtitlan
en.text:
On 13 August 1521, after a siege of about three months, the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan fell to Spanish conquistadors led by Hernán Cortés and their many Indigenous allies. The last Aztec ruler, Cuauhtémoc, was captured as he tried to escape by canoe.

Tenochtitlan was one of the largest cities in the world, home to perhaps 200,000 people. It was built on an island in Lake Texcoco, connected to the shore by long causeways, with canals, floating gardens called chinampas, markets, and the great twin temple of the Templo Mayor at its centre. Spanish soldiers wrote that it was more magnificent than any city they had seen in Europe.

The Mexica, as the Aztecs called themselves, ruled an empire that demanded tribute from many conquered peoples. Many of those peoples hated Aztec rule. Cortés, who landed in 1519 with only a few hundred Spaniards, gained tens of thousands of allies, especially from the city-state of Tlaxcala.

The Spanish were at first welcomed into the city by the emperor Moctezuma II, who was then taken prisoner and died in 1520. The Spanish were driven out, but returned with allies and boats built for the lake.

A smallpox epidemic, brought by the Europeans, had already killed huge numbers in the city, including Moctezuma's successor Cuitláhuac. The siege cut off food and water, and much of the city was destroyed in the fighting.

Mexico City was built on its ruins. The Templo Mayor was rediscovered in 1978 by electricity workers, and the eagle on a cactus, the symbol of Tenochtitlan's founding, is on Mexico's flag today.

en.title: The transatlantic slave trade
en.place: West and Central Africa to the Americas
en.text:
Around 1526, the first known ship carried enslaved Africans directly from Africa to the Americas. Over the next three and a half centuries, about 12.5 million African women, men and children were forced onto ships bound across the Atlantic. Around 10.7 million survived the voyage.

Europeans, especially the Portuguese, British, French, Spanish and Dutch, built forts and trading posts along the coast of West and Central Africa, such as Elmina in Ghana and Gorée in Senegal. They traded cloth, guns, alcohol and metal goods to African rulers and merchants in exchange for captives, many taken in wars and raids that the trade itself encouraged.

The journey across the ocean was called the Middle Passage. People were chained below deck in crowded, dark and filthy holds for weeks or months. Disease, violence and despair killed many. Some resisted, through revolts on board or by refusing to eat.

In the Americas, enslaved people were forced to work on plantations of sugar, tobacco, cotton and coffee, in mines and in houses. Brazil received the largest number, followed by the Caribbean. Their labour produced enormous wealth for Europe and the Americas.

Enslaved Africans resisted constantly: through escape, rebellion, preserving languages, music, religion and family. Their cultures shaped the Americas, from samba and jazz to food and faith.

The trade was abolished step by step in the nineteenth century, after campaigns by abolitionists and above all the resistance of enslaved people, including the Haitian Revolution. Its effects, including racism and inequality, are still felt on both sides of the Atlantic.

en.title: Queen Nzinga comes to power
en.text:
In 1624 Nzinga Mbande became ruler of Ndongo, a kingdom of the Mbundu people in what is now Angola. For nearly four decades she resisted Portuguese colonial expansion and the slave trade that came with it, becoming one of the most famous leaders in African history.

Portugal had established a colony at Luanda in 1575 and pushed inland, raiding for captives to ship to Brazil. Nzinga first appeared in history in 1622 as an ambassador sent by her brother, King Ngola Mbandi, to negotiate with the Portuguese governor in Luanda.

A famous story tells that when she entered the room, the governor sat on a chair but offered her only a mat on the floor. Nzinga signalled to a servant, who knelt on hands and knees, and she sat on the servant's back, speaking to the governor as an equal.

After her brother's death she took power, though some men argued a woman could not rule. When the Portuguese backed rivals, she moved east and conquered the kingdom of Matamba, building a new power base. She formed alliances with the Imbangala warriors and even with the Dutch, who were fighting Portugal.

She was a skilled diplomat and military commander, leading troops into battle into her sixties. In 1657 she finally signed a peace treaty with Portugal. She died in 1663, aged about 80.

Nzinga's legacy is complex, as her kingdoms were also involved in the slave trade, as most powers of the region were. But in Angola today she is honoured as a national heroine and symbol of resistance.

en.title: The Tokugawa shogunate begins
en.text:
On 24 March 1603, Tokugawa Ieyasu received the title of shogun from the emperor of Japan. He set up his government in the small castle town of Edo, today's Tokyo, beginning more than 250 years of peace known as the Edo period.

For over a century before, Japan had been torn by civil war between rival warlords, the daimyo. Three great leaders gradually reunited the country: Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and finally Tokugawa Ieyasu, who defeated his rivals at the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600.

The emperor in Kyoto remained a sacred figure, but real power belonged to the shogun. The Tokugawa controlled the daimyo through a clever system: each lord had to spend every other year in Edo and leave his family there as hostages. The costly journeys kept the daimyo busy and loyal.

Society was organised into ranks: samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Christianity was banned after a rebellion in 1637, and from the 1630s the shogunate restricted foreign contact. Only Dutch and Chinese traders were allowed, at Nagasaki.

Yet Japan flourished. Edo grew into one of the largest cities in the world, with perhaps a million people. Literacy spread. Kabuki theatre, haiku poetry, and woodblock prints such as Hokusai's "Great Wave" were born in this era.

In 1853 American warships under Commodore Matthew Perry arrived and forced Japan to open to trade. The shogunate collapsed in 1868, power returned to the emperor in the Meiji Restoration, and Japan rapidly modernised.

en.title: The American Declaration of Independence
en.text:
On 4 July 1776, delegates of thirteen British colonies in North America, meeting in Philadelphia, adopted the Declaration of Independence. They announced that the colonies were now free and independent states: the United States of America.

Tensions with Britain had grown for more than a decade over taxes imposed by the British Parliament, in which the colonists had no representatives. The slogan "no taxation without representation" spread. Fighting began in April 1775 at Lexington and Concord in Massachusetts.

The Declaration was drafted mainly by Thomas Jefferson. Its most famous lines state that all men are created equal and have rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and that governments get their power from the consent of the governed.

Those words were powerful but did not apply to everyone. Jefferson himself enslaved more than 600 people during his life, and around one in five people in the colonies were enslaved Africans and their descendants. Women could not vote, and Native American nations were treated as enemies. Black Americans such as Frederick Douglass later used the Declaration's own words to demand freedom.

With help from France, Spain and the Netherlands, the Americans won the war, which ended in 1783. The Constitution, written in 1787, created a federal republic with an elected president.

The Declaration inspired revolutions elsewhere, including in France, Haiti and Latin America. Its promise of equality took centuries more of struggle, through the abolition of slavery and the civil rights movement, to begin to be fulfilled.

en.title: The storming of the Bastille
en.text:
On 14 July 1789, a crowd in Paris attacked the Bastille, a royal fortress and prison and a hated symbol of the king's power. After hours of fighting, the governor surrendered. The fall of the Bastille became the symbol of the French Revolution.

France was in crisis. The government was bankrupt after expensive wars, including support for the American Revolution. Bad harvests made bread so expensive that poor families went hungry. Society was divided into three estates: the clergy, the nobility, and everyone else, the Third Estate, who paid most of the taxes but had little power.

In May 1789 King Louis XVI called the Estates-General to raise money. The Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly, claiming to represent the nation. When troops gathered around Paris, people feared the king would crush the assembly, and they rose up.

In August the Assembly abolished feudal privileges and adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, proclaiming liberty, equality before the law and sovereignty of the nation.

The revolution became more radical. France became a republic in 1792, and the king was executed in 1793. During the Reign of Terror, thousands were guillotined. In 1799 the general Napoleon Bonaparte seized power.

The revolution spread ideas of citizenship, rights and nationalism across Europe and beyond. In 1794 France abolished slavery in its colonies, under pressure from the revolt in Saint-Domingue, though Napoleon later restored it. 14 July is France's national day.

en.title: Haiti declares independence
en.text:
On 1 January 1804, at Gonaïves, General Jean-Jacques Dessalines declared the independence of Haiti. It was the first nation in the world founded by formerly enslaved people who had freed themselves, and the second independent country in the Americas.

The French colony of Saint-Domingue was the richest colony in the world, producing much of Europe's sugar and coffee. Its wealth came from the brutal labour of around half a million enslaved Africans, who greatly outnumbered the white colonists.

In August 1791, enslaved people in the north rose up in a massive, well-planned revolt, said to have begun after a ceremony at Bois Caïman. Over the following years, a brilliant leader emerged: Toussaint Louverture, a formerly enslaved man who became a general, diplomat and governor. He defeated British and Spanish forces, and in 1794 France abolished slavery.

In 1802 Napoleon sent a huge army to restore slavery. Toussaint was captured by trickery and died in a French prison in 1803. But Haitian forces under Dessalines and Henri Christophe, helped by yellow fever that devastated the French troops, won the decisive Battle of Vertières in November 1803.

The new nation took the Taíno name Ayiti, "land of mountains".

Haiti's freedom terrified slaveholding nations. It was isolated for decades, and in 1825 France forced Haiti, under threat of invasion, to pay a huge sum as "compensation" to former slaveholders. Paying this debt drained Haiti's economy for over a century. Yet the revolution inspired enslaved people and independence movements across the Americas.

en.title: The first modern railway opens
en.text:
On 15 September 1830, the Liverpool and Manchester Railway opened in England. It was the first railway to run entirely on steam locomotives, on a double track, carrying both passengers and goods on a timetable between two major cities. It marked the start of the railway age.

The Industrial Revolution had begun in Britain in the eighteenth century. Machines powered by water and then steam transformed the making of cloth, iron and many other goods. James Watt's improved steam engines, from the 1770s, made steam power practical.

Factories in Manchester needed raw cotton from the port of Liverpool, and canals were slow and expensive. Engineers George Stephenson and his son Robert built the railway, cutting through rock and crossing a peat bog. In trials in 1829, their locomotive Rocket won against rival engines, reaching speeds of around 48 kilometres per hour.

The opening day was also marked by tragedy. William Huskisson, a member of parliament, stepped onto the track and was struck by Rocket, becoming one of the first widely reported railway fatalities.

The railway was a huge success. Within decades, railways spread across Britain, Europe, North America, India and beyond. They moved goods and people faster and cheaper than ever, created national time zones, and changed where people lived and worked.

In Africa, colonial railways were built mainly to carry raw materials to ports. The Uganda Railway from Mombasa and the Central Line from Dar es Salaam to Kigoma, finished in 1914, still shape East Africa's transport today. The Industrial Revolution's reliance on coal also began the rise in carbon emissions behind today's climate change.

en.title: The First World War ends
en.text:
At 11 a.m. on 11 November 1918, the guns fell silent on the Western Front. Germany had signed an armistice with the Allies in a railway carriage in the forest of Compiègne, France, early that morning. The First World War, then called the Great War, was over.

The war began in 1914 after the assassination of the Austrian Archduke Franz Ferdinand in Sarajevo. A system of alliances drew in the great powers: Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire on one side; France, Britain, Russia, later Italy and the United States, on the other.

In Western Europe, armies dug lines of trenches from the North Sea to Switzerland. New weapons, including machine guns, heavy artillery, poison gas, tanks and aircraft, made battles like the Somme and Verdun enormously deadly. About 9 million soldiers and millions of civilians died.

The war was also fought in Africa. In German East Africa, today's Tanzania, Burundi and Rwanda, German commander Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck fought a long campaign against British, South African, Indian, Belgian and Portuguese forces. Hundreds of thousands of African porters, the carrier corps, were forced to carry supplies, and tens of thousands died of disease, hunger and exhaustion. In fact, fighting in East Africa continued until news of the armistice arrived, and Lettow-Vorbeck surrendered in Northern Rhodesia on 25 November.

The peace treaties redrew the map. Empires collapsed, and Germany's colonies were given to the victors, which is how Tanganyika came under British rule. The harsh Treaty of Versailles helped create the conditions for the Second World War. 11 November is remembered as Armistice or Remembrance Day.

en.title: The Second World War begins
en.text:
At dawn on 1 September 1939, German forces invaded Poland. Two days later, Britain and France declared war on Germany. The Second World War, the deadliest conflict in human history, had begun.

Germany was ruled by Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party, who had come to power in 1933 promising to undo the Treaty of Versailles and build a racially "pure" empire. Germany rearmed, took over Austria in 1938 and Czechoslovakia in 1939, while Britain and France at first tried to avoid war by giving in to demands.

The war spread across the world. Germany conquered much of Europe and invaded the Soviet Union in 1941. Japan, allied with Germany and Italy, had been at war in China since 1937, and in December 1941 attacked the US fleet at Pearl Harbor, bringing the United States into the war.

The Nazis carried out the Holocaust, the systematic murder of six million Jews, as well as Roma, disabled people and others. Cities were bombed, and civilians suffered terribly in every theatre of war.

Africa was deeply involved. Battles were fought in North Africa and in Ethiopia, which had been occupied by Italy in 1936 and was freed in 1941. More than a million African soldiers served, including in the King's African Rifles from Tanganyika, Kenya and Uganda, fighting in Ethiopia, Madagascar and Burma.

The war ended in Europe in May 1945 and in Asia in August, after atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. Around 70 to 85 million people died. The war led to the founding of the United Nations, the Cold War, and a new wave of independence movements in Africa and Asia.

en.title: The United Nations is founded
en.place: San Francisco and New York, United States
en.text:
On 24 October 1945, the Charter of the United Nations came into force after being ratified by most of its 51 founding members. The new organisation was meant, in the words of its Charter, to save future generations from the scourge of war.

The Charter was signed in San Francisco in June 1945, as the Second World War was ending. An earlier organisation, the League of Nations, had failed to stop the war. The UN was designed to be stronger.

All member states sit in the General Assembly, each with one vote. The Security Council has 15 members, five of them permanent: the United States, the Soviet Union (now Russia), Britain, France and China. Each permanent member can veto decisions, a system that has often blocked action.

Only four African countries were founding members: Egypt, Ethiopia, Liberia and South Africa. As colonies won independence, the number of African members grew quickly. Today there are 193 member states, and 54 of them are African.

The UN played a role in African independence. Tanganyika was a UN trust territory, and Julius Nyerere spoke before the UN in 1955. The UN also isolated apartheid South Africa.

In 1948 the UN adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. Its agencies, such as UNICEF, the World Health Organization and the World Food Programme, work on health, children's rights and hunger. UN peacekeepers have served in dozens of conflicts.

The UN is often criticised for being slow and for the power of the veto. But for 80 years it has remained the main place where all the world's nations meet. 24 October is United Nations Day.

en.title: India and Pakistan become independent
en.text:
At midnight between 14 and 15 August 1947, British rule in India ended. India's first prime minister, Jawaharlal Nehru, told the assembly that at the stroke of the midnight hour, while the world slept, India would awake to life and freedom. A day earlier, Pakistan had become a separate independent state.

Britain had ruled much of South Asia for nearly two centuries, first through the East India Company and, after a great uprising in 1857, directly under the Crown. India's wealth in cotton, tea and other goods enriched Britain, while famines killed millions under colonial rule.

The Indian National Congress, founded in 1885, led the independence movement. Its most famous leader was Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi, called Mahatma, "great soul". Gandhi had developed his methods of non-violent resistance, satyagraha, while living in South Africa from 1893 to 1914, fighting discrimination against Indians there. In India he led mass campaigns such as the Salt March of 1930.

As independence approached, tension grew between Hindus and Muslims. The Muslim League, led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah, demanded a separate state. The British divided the land, creating India and Pakistan, whose eastern part later became Bangladesh in 1971.

Partition caused one of the largest migrations in history. Some 15 million people crossed the new borders, and hundreds of thousands, perhaps up to two million, were killed in communal violence. Gandhi himself was assassinated in January 1948.

India's independence inspired African nationalists, including Kwame Nkrumah and Julius Nyerere, who studied Gandhi's ideas of non-violent struggle.

en.title: The structure of DNA is revealed
en.text:
On 25 April 1953, the science journal Nature published a short paper by James Watson and Francis Crick describing the structure of DNA: a double helix, like a twisted ladder. It explained how living things store and copy the instructions for life.

DNA, deoxyribonucleic acid, had been known since the nineteenth century, and by the 1940s experiments suggested it carried genetic information. But nobody knew how.

At King's College London, Rosalind Franklin, a brilliant chemist, used X-rays to take extremely sharp images of DNA fibres. Her famous "Photograph 51" showed a pattern that pointed to a helix. Her colleague Maurice Wilkins showed the image to Watson without Franklin's knowledge, and her measurements, shared through a report, were crucial to Watson and Crick's model.

The model showed two strands winding around each other, connected by pairs of chemical bases: adenine with thymine, guanine with cytosine. Because each base fits only its partner, each strand can serve as a template to copy the other. Watson and Crick noted, in a famous understatement, that this suggested a copying mechanism for genetic material.

Watson, Crick and Wilkins received the Nobel Prize in 1962. Franklin had died of cancer in 1958, aged 37, and Nobel Prizes are not given after death. Her role is now widely recognised.

The discovery opened the way to modern biology and medicine: genetic testing, DNA fingerprinting, the Human Genome Project completed in 2003, and gene-based vaccines. It also helped confirm, from African fossils and genes, that all modern humans originated in Africa.

en.title: Sputnik, the first artificial satellite
en.text:
On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first human-made object to orbit the Earth. It was a shiny metal ball just 58 centimetres wide, with four long antennas, and it beeped a simple radio signal that anyone with a radio receiver could hear.

Sputnik circled the Earth about every 96 minutes. People around the world went outside at night to watch the rocket that had carried it, glinting as it passed overhead. Its batteries died after three weeks, and in January 1958 it fell back into the atmosphere and burned up.

The satellite was launched by an R-7 rocket, originally designed to carry nuclear weapons across continents. That frightened the United States: if the Soviets could put a satellite into orbit, they could also reach American cities.

The shock started the space race. The United States launched its own first satellite, Explorer 1, in January 1958, and created NASA. It also poured money into science and mathematics education.

A month after Sputnik 1, the Soviets launched Sputnik 2 carrying a dog named Laika, the first animal to orbit the Earth. She did not survive the flight. In 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first human in space, and in 1969 Americans landed on the Moon.

Today thousands of satellites orbit the Earth. They give us weather forecasts, GPS navigation, television, internet links and mobile phone banking, and monitor droughts, forests and floods across Africa. All of that began with one small beeping ball in 1957.

en.title: The March on Washington
en.text:
On 28 August 1963, around 250,000 people gathered at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C., demanding jobs and freedom for Black Americans. There, Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech, one of the most famous speeches in history.

A century after slavery was abolished in the United States, Black Americans in many states still faced segregation laws, known as Jim Crow. Schools, buses, restaurants and even water fountains were separated by race. Black citizens were often blocked from voting, and many faced violence, including lynching.

The civil rights movement fought back with courage and organisation. In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery, Alabama, starting a year-long bus boycott led by a young pastor, Martin Luther King Jr. Students held sit-ins at segregated lunch counters, and Freedom Riders challenged segregated buses.

The march was organised by leaders including A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin. It was peaceful, and included Black and white Americans, workers, students, churches and celebrities.

King spoke of a dream that his four children would one day live in a nation where they would be judged not by the colour of their skin but by the content of their character.

The march helped pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which outlawed segregation, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965. King received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in 1968. The American movement was closely connected with African independence struggles, and leaders on both sides of the Atlantic inspired each other.

en.title: The World Wide Web goes public
en.text:
On 6 August 1991, a British computer scientist named Tim Berners-Lee posted a message on an online discussion group describing a project called the WorldWideWeb, and invited others to use it. The first website, explaining what the Web was and how to use it, was already running on a computer at CERN, the European physics laboratory near Geneva.

The internet, a network linking computer networks, had grown from American research projects since the late 1960s. But it was hard to use. Berners-Lee wanted a simple way for scientists to share documents, linking them together so a reader could jump from one to another.

In 1989 he proposed a system of hypertext. By the end of 1990 he had created the three key parts of the Web: HTML, the language for writing web pages; HTTP, the rules for sending them; and URLs, the addresses that find them. He also wrote the first web browser and web server.

Crucially, CERN made the Web's technology free for anyone to use in 1993, without patents or fees. That openness allowed it to grow incredibly fast. Graphical browsers like Mosaic made it easy for ordinary people.

Today more than five billion people use the internet. In Africa, mobile phones brought most people online, and innovations such as M-Pesa mobile money, launched in Kenya in 2007, changed how millions save and pay.

The Web also brought new problems: misinformation, online abuse and threats to privacy. Berners-Lee has campaigned to keep the Web open, safe and available to everyone. The site you are using now runs on his invention.

en.title: The genocide against the Tutsi in Rwanda
en.text:
On 7 April 1994, the day after the plane carrying Rwanda's president Juvénal Habyarimana was shot down over Kigali, organised killings began across Rwanda. In about 100 days, extremist militias, soldiers and ordinary people incited by hate propaganda murdered around 800,000 to one million people, most of them Tutsi, along with moderate Hutu who opposed the killing.

Under Belgian colonial rule, divisions between Hutu and Tutsi had been hardened: Belgium issued identity cards stating each person's group and favoured one group over the other. After independence, waves of violence forced many Tutsi into exile. In 1990 the Rwandan Patriotic Front (RPF), formed mostly by Tutsi exiles, invaded from Uganda, and civil war followed.

Extremists prepared for mass murder in advance. A radio station, RTLM, spread hatred, calling Tutsi "cockroaches" and later broadcasting names and locations of people to be killed. Militias called the Interahamwe were armed and trained. Neighbours were turned against neighbours; many victims were killed in churches and schools where they had sought safety.

The world failed Rwanda. A small UN peacekeeping force was there, but most of it was withdrawn, and major powers refused to call it genocide or intervene.

The genocide ended in July 1994 when the RPF defeated the government forces. Rwanda has since rebuilt, holding community courts called gacaca to try hundreds of thousands of cases.

Each year, from 7 April, Rwanda observes Kwibuka, "remember". Memorials such as the Kigali Genocide Memorial ask the world never to forget, and to act against hate before it becomes murder.

en.title: South Africa's first democratic election
en.text:
On 27 April 1994, millions of South Africans stood in queues that stretched for kilometres, many waiting for hours in the sun. For most of them, it was the first time in their lives they were allowed to vote. Apartheid was ending.

For nearly 50 years under apartheid, and centuries of colonial rule before it, South Africa's Black majority had been denied political rights. Laws decided where people could live, work, study and whom they could marry, based on race. Millions were forcibly moved to "homelands".

Resistance took many forms: the ANC's Defiance Campaign, the Freedom Charter of 1955, the Soweto student uprising of 1976, trade union strikes, international boycotts and an armed struggle. Neighbouring countries, including Tanzania, supported the liberation movements at great cost.

After Nelson Mandela's release in 1990, negotiations between the government and the liberation movements led to an interim constitution. The road was violent; thousands died in political conflict, and the country came close to civil war. The assassination of the popular leader Chris Hani in 1993 nearly derailed the process, until Mandela appealed for calm.

Over four days of voting, nearly 20 million people cast ballots. The ANC won about 62 percent of the vote, and on 10 May 1994 Nelson Mandela was inaugurated as president, with leaders from around the world watching.

27 April is celebrated as Freedom Day. South Africa's new constitution of 1996 is admired worldwide for its bill of rights, though deep inequality from the apartheid era still challenges the country.

en.title: Wangari Maathai wins the Nobel Peace Prize
en.text:
On 8 October 2004, the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that the Nobel Peace Prize would go to Wangari Maathai of Kenya, "for her contribution to sustainable development, democracy and peace". She became the first African woman to win a Nobel Prize.

Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in Nyeri, in Kenya's central highlands. She won a scholarship to study in the United States, and in 1971 became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate, in veterinary anatomy, at the University of Nairobi.

Rural women told her their streams were drying up, firewood was harder to find, and food was scarce. She saw that cutting down forests was at the root of these problems. In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, which paid women a small sum to plant and care for tree seedlings. Over the decades the movement planted more than 50 million trees in Kenya.

Planting trees led her into politics. She challenged the government of President Daniel arap Moi when it tried to build a skyscraper in Nairobi's Uhuru Park and to give away public forest land. She was beaten, arrested and called a troublemaker, but she did not stop. She campaigned for democracy and the release of political prisoners.

In 2002 she was elected to parliament and became assistant minister for the environment.

Maathai died in 2011. She often told a story of a hummingbird carrying drops of water to a forest fire, saying: "I will be a hummingbird. I will do the best I can." Her message linked the environment, women's rights and peace.

en.title: COVID-19 is declared a pandemic
en.text:
On 11 March 2020, the World Health Organization declared that the outbreak of a new coronavirus disease, COVID-19, had become a pandemic. Within weeks, much of the world had closed schools, offices and borders.

The virus, called SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in Wuhan, China, in December 2019. It spread through tiny droplets and particles in the air when infected people breathed, spoke or coughed. Many people had mild illness, but it could cause severe pneumonia, especially in older people and those with other conditions.

Hospitals in many countries were overwhelmed. Governments imposed lockdowns, asking people to stay home. Face masks, hand-washing and keeping distance became part of daily life. Millions lost work, and children missed months of school. Online meetings and remote work spread fast.

Scientists worked at extraordinary speed. Vaccines, including new mRNA vaccines built on decades of research, were developed, tested and approved within about a year, by December 2020. Billions of doses were given worldwide.

But vaccines were shared unequally. Rich countries received them first, while many African countries waited months. African scientists played key roles; in late 2021, researchers in South Africa and Botswana were the first to identify and report the Omicron variant, quickly alerting the world.

WHO estimates that the pandemic caused around 7 million confirmed deaths and many more excess deaths, perhaps over 15 million in its first two years. In May 2023 WHO declared that COVID-19 was no longer a global health emergency. The pandemic showed how connected the world is, and how much we depend on science, health workers and cooperation.

en.title: The Epic of Gilgamesh
en.text:
The Epic of Gilgamesh is one of the oldest great stories in the world. Poems about Gilgamesh were written in Sumerian around 2100 BCE, and the best-known version, on twelve clay tablets, was found in the ruined library of the Assyrian king Ashurbanipal at Nineveh.

Gilgamesh was king of Uruk, two-thirds god and one-third human. He was strong and proud, and he oppressed his people. The gods answered their prayers by creating Enkidu, a wild man who lived among the animals. Enkidu was tamed by contact with people, came to the city, and wrestled Gilgamesh. Neither could defeat the other, and they became the closest of friends.

Together they travelled to the great Cedar Forest and killed its guardian monster, Humbaba. When the goddess Ishtar offered to marry Gilgamesh and he insulted her, she sent the Bull of Heaven to destroy Uruk. The friends killed the bull too. As punishment, the gods decided that Enkidu must die.

Heartbroken, Gilgamesh wandered the wilderness, terrified of his own death. He searched for Utnapishtim, the only man granted eternal life. Utnapishtim told him the story of a great flood sent by the gods, which he survived by building a boat and taking animals aboard, a story strikingly similar to the later story of Noah.

Utnapishtim showed Gilgamesh a plant that restored youth, but a snake stole it while Gilgamesh bathed. He returned to Uruk empty-handed. Looking at the city's great walls, he understood that people live on through what they build and how they are remembered.

The epic asks the oldest human questions: about friendship, grief, and how to live knowing that we must die.

en.title: Isis and Osiris
en.text:
The story of Osiris and Isis was one of the most important myths of ancient Egypt. Its elements appear in the Pyramid Texts of around 2400 BCE, and a full version was later written by the Greek writer Plutarch.

Osiris was a wise and good king who taught the Egyptians to farm, to make laws and to honour the gods. His wife, the goddess Isis, was clever and powerful in magic. But their brother Set, god of storms, deserts and chaos, was jealous.

Set held a feast and brought a beautiful chest, promising it to whoever fit inside perfectly. When Osiris lay down in it, Set slammed the lid, sealed it with lead and threw it into the Nile. The chest floated out to sea and came to rest at Byblos, where a great tree grew around it.

Isis searched the world for her husband and brought his body home. But Set found it and tore it into fourteen pieces, scattering them across Egypt. Isis and her sister Nephthys searched again and gathered every piece. With the help of the jackal-headed god Anubis, they wrapped the body in linen, making the first mummy, and Isis breathed life into Osiris long enough to conceive a son, Horus.

Osiris could not return to the living. He became king of the underworld, judging the souls of the dead. Isis hid Horus in the papyrus marshes of the Nile delta, and when he grew up he fought Set for the throne of Egypt, and won.

Every pharaoh was seen as Horus in life and Osiris in death. The yearly flooding of the Nile, bringing new life to the fields, was linked to Osiris's rebirth.

en.title: Kintu and Nambi: the first people of Buganda
en.text:
The Baganda people of Uganda tell how the first man, Kintu, came to their land. He lived alone with only his cow, drinking its milk for food.

One day Nambi, the daughter of Ggulu, the ruler of the sky, came down to earth with her brothers. She saw Kintu and loved him, and wished to marry him. But her father and brothers doubted that this poor, lonely man was worthy. Ggulu set Kintu a series of impossible tests.

Kintu was told to eat an enormous meal prepared for a hundred people; he hid most of it in a hole in the ground. He was told to split a rock with a copper axe; he found a rock already cracked. He was told to fill a pot with dew; at dawn he found the pot filled. Finally he had to pick out his own cow from a vast herd. A bee whispered to him to watch which cow it landed on, and so he chose correctly, even finding the calves his cow had borne.

Ggulu was impressed and allowed the marriage. But he warned the couple to leave at once and never return, because Nambi's brother Walumbe, whose name means Death, would want to follow them.

On the journey Nambi remembered that she had forgotten millet to feed her chicken. Against Kintu's pleading, she went back. Walumbe saw her and followed them to earth.

Kintu and Nambi had many children, but Walumbe began taking them away. Ggulu sent another son, Kayikuuzi, to capture him, but Walumbe hid in the earth. And so, the Baganda say, death came into the world.

In Buganda tradition, Kintu is also remembered as the first king, the ancestor of the kabakas.

en.title: Anansi and the box of stories
en.text:
Among the Akan peoples of Ghana, Kwaku Anansi, the spider, is the great trickster. He is small and often lazy, but he is clever enough to outwit creatures far larger than himself. One of the best-known tales explains how all stories came to belong to him.

Long ago, all the stories in the world belonged to Nyame, the sky god, who kept them in a box. Anansi climbed up his web to the sky and asked to buy them. Nyame laughed. Many great and powerful beings had tried. The price, he said, was to bring him four creatures: Onini the python, Osebo the leopard, Mmoboro the hornets, and Mmoatia, a fairy whom no one could see.

Anansi went home and made plans with his wife, Aso. He went to the python and argued loudly with himself about whether the snake was longer than a palm branch. Proud Onini lay down along the branch to prove it, and Anansi tied him to it.

He dug a pit on the leopard's path, and when Osebo fell in, offered to help him out, then tied him up. He poured water over the hornets' nest and told them it was raining, inviting them into a dry gourd, which he then sealed. For Mmoatia he carved a doll, covered it in sticky gum and placed a bowl of mashed yam before it. The fairy ate the yam, and when the doll did not thank her, she slapped it and became stuck.

Anansi brought all four to Nyame, and the sky god kept his word. From that day, the stories were called Anansesem, spider stories.

Carried across the Atlantic by enslaved Africans, Anansi stories are still told in Jamaica, the Caribbean and the Americas.

en.title: Fumo Liongo, hero of the Swahili coast
en.place: Pate and Shanga, Lamu archipelago, Kenya
en.text:
Fumo Liongo is the greatest hero of Swahili legend. He is remembered as a warrior and poet from the Lamu archipelago on the northern Swahili coast. Some historians think he may have been a real ruler who lived sometime between the thirteenth and seventeenth centuries; around him grew one of East Africa's most beloved epics.

Liongo was said to be enormously tall and strong, able to shoot arrows with deadly aim and to walk across the land faster than any man. He was the rightful heir to the throne of Pate, but because his mother was not the chief wife, the throne passed to his cousin, the Sultan Daudi Mringwari.

The Sultan feared Liongo's popularity and tried again and again to kill him. Liongo was captured and chained in prison. His mother sent him food every day. One day she sent a loaf of bread with a file hidden inside it. While the guards were distracted by music and dancing that Liongo himself requested, he filed through his chains, burst free and escaped into the forest.

Liongo had a secret: he could not be killed by any ordinary weapon. Only a copper needle driven into his navel could kill him. The Sultan persuaded Liongo's own son, or in some versions his nephew, to learn the secret and betray him. One night the young man stabbed Liongo as he slept.

Liongo did not fall. He walked to the town well, knelt with his bow drawn, and died there. For days the people were too afraid to approach to fetch water, believing he was still alive.

Liongo is also remembered as a poet. Songs and poems attributed to him are among the oldest works of Swahili literature.

en.title: Kibo and Mawenzi: the legend of Kilimanjaro
en.text:
The Chagga people, who live on the green slopes of Kilimanjaro, tell a story to explain why the mountain's two great peaks look so different. Kibo is broad, smooth and crowned with snow. Mawenzi is jagged, broken and sharp.

Long ago, the story says, Kibo and Mawenzi were two neighbours, like sisters or brothers living side by side. Kibo was careful and hard-working. She always kept her fire burning and her granary full. Mawenzi was careless and often let his fire go out.

One day Mawenzi's fire died, and he went to Kibo to borrow some embers. Kibo gave him fire generously, and also some bananas to eat. Mawenzi enjoyed the bananas so much that, on the way home, he deliberately put out the fire, so that he could go back for more.

He returned and asked again. Kibo gave him fire again, and more food. A third time Mawenzi let his fire die and came back asking. This time Kibo lost her patience. She seized her pestle, the heavy wooden pole used for pounding grain, and beat Mawenzi so hard that his head was shattered into pieces.

That, the Chagga say, is why Mawenzi's peak is broken and jagged to this day, while Kibo stands tall and calm, and why Mawenzi seems to hide his face in shame behind the clouds.

The story teaches about neighbourliness: generosity is a virtue, but taking advantage of a kind neighbour is shameful. It also shows how the mountain was not only a landscape for the Chagga, but a living part of their moral world. Kilimanjaro, sometimes called Kilema Kyaro in Chagga, is still at the centre of their stories.

en.title: Enkai and the gift of cattle
en.text:
The Maasai people of Kenya and Tanzania believe in one God, Enkai, sometimes written Engai. Enkai has two natures: Enkai Narok, the black God, who is kind and brings the rain that makes grass grow; and Enkai Nanyokie, the red God, who is angry and brings drought and lightning.

A Maasai story tells how the people received their cattle. Long ago, the sky and the earth were joined, and Enkai lived close to people. Then the sky and earth were separated. The Maasai would have been left with nothing, so Enkai sent cattle down from the sky on a long rope, made from the aerial roots of a wild fig tree, for a man named Naiteru-kop, a name meaning "the one who began the earth".

The cattle came down and the people were happy. But a jealous hunting people, the Dorobo, who had not received cattle, cut the rope. The gift from the sky stopped forever.

From this story the Maasai believe that all cattle in the world were given to them by Enkai. For this reason, in the past, Maasai warriors felt justified in taking cattle from other peoples, believing they were only returning cattle to their rightful owners.

Cattle are at the heart of Maasai life. They provide milk, meat and blood for food, hides for bedding and sandals, and wealth for marriage. Children are blessed with cattle, and greetings often ask about the herds as well as the family.

Mount Ol Doinyo Lengai, an active volcano in northern Tanzania, is called "the Mountain of God". The Maasai traditionally pray toward it, and its eruptions are understood as signs of Enkai's mood.

en.title: Mami Wata, spirit of the waters
en.text:
Mami Wata, whose name comes from "Mother Water", is a powerful water spirit honoured in many parts of West and Central Africa, and in the African diaspora in the Americas. She is often pictured as a beautiful woman with long flowing hair, sometimes with the tail of a fish or holding a snake.

Belief in water spirits in Africa is very old. Rivers, lakes and the sea give life through water and fish, but they also take life in floods and drownings. Many peoples, such as the Yoruba, Igbo, Ewe and Efik, honoured spirits of particular waters. Over centuries of trade along the Atlantic coast, these beliefs mixed with images brought by foreign sailors, such as mermaids and figureheads. The popular picture of Mami Wata with long hair and a snake around her shoulders probably comes from a nineteenth-century European print of a snake charmer, which became widely copied in Africa.

Mami Wata is believed to bring wealth, beauty, healing and good fortune to those she favours. But she is also dangerous and jealous. Stories tell of people who disappear while swimming and return years later, rich and wise, or who make pacts with her and must remain faithful.

Her followers often dress in red and white, and offer her perfume, sweets, mirrors, combs and other beautiful things. Shrines are decorated with images of her.

Today Mami Wata appears in Nollywood films, popular songs, paintings and sculptures, from Lagos to Kinshasa to Haiti. She reflects how African beliefs have adapted to change while keeping their deep respect for the power of water.

en.title: Prometheus steals fire
en.text:
In the myths of ancient Greece, told by the poet Hesiod around 700 BCE, the Titan Prometheus was the great friend of humankind. His name means "forethought".

When the world was young, the gods of Mount Olympus, led by Zeus, defeated the older Titans and took power. Prometheus had sided with Zeus, but he cared deeply for the humans who lived on earth, cold, weak and without skills.

At a feast at Mekone, Prometheus tricked Zeus. He divided a sacrificed ox into two portions: the good meat hidden inside the unappetising stomach, and the bones wrapped in shining fat. Zeus chose the attractive portion and found only bones. From then on, the Greeks said, humans kept the meat of sacrifices and burned the bones for the gods.

In anger, Zeus hid fire from humanity. Prometheus climbed to the heavens, lit a fennel stalk from the fire of the gods, and carried it hidden down to earth. With fire, humans could cook, keep warm, work metal and build civilisation.

Zeus's punishment was terrible. He had Prometheus chained to a rock in the Caucasus mountains, where every day an eagle came to eat his liver, which grew back each night. After many generations, the hero Heracles killed the eagle and freed him.

Zeus also punished humans by creating Pandora, the first woman in Greek myth, who opened a jar that released sickness, toil and sorrow into the world, leaving only hope inside.

Prometheus became a symbol of rebellion for the sake of knowledge and human progress. Mary Shelley subtitled her novel Frankenstein "The Modern Prometheus".

en.title: The Trojan War and the wooden horse
en.text:
The story of the Trojan War was told by the Greek poet Homer around 750 BCE in the Iliad and the Odyssey, and by many later writers. It is one of the most influential stories in Western literature.

It began, the myth says, with a golden apple marked "for the fairest". Three goddesses, Hera, Athena and Aphrodite, each claimed it, and Paris, a prince of Troy, was asked to choose. Aphrodite promised him the most beautiful woman in the world, and he chose her. That woman was Helen, wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta. Paris carried Helen away to Troy.

Menelaus's brother Agamemnon gathered a huge Greek army and a thousand ships. Among the heroes were Odysseus, the cleverest, and Achilles, the greatest warrior, who could only be wounded in his heel. For ten years the Greeks besieged Troy's strong walls.

The Iliad tells of a few weeks in the tenth year: Achilles' anger at Agamemnon, the death of his friend Patroclus at the hands of the Trojan prince Hector, and Achilles' revenge. It ends with Hector's father, old King Priam, coming alone to beg Achilles for his son's body, and the two enemies weeping together.

Troy finally fell through a trick devised by Odysseus. The Greeks built a giant wooden horse, hid soldiers inside, and pretended to sail away. The Trojans dragged the horse into the city as a trophy. At night the soldiers climbed out and opened the gates.

Archaeologists have found the ruins of a real city at Hisarlik in Turkey, destroyed more than once in the Bronze Age. Whether a real war inspired the legend is still debated.

en.title: Ragnarök: the twilight of the gods
en.text:
The Norse peoples of Scandinavia told of a final battle at the end of the world, Ragnarök, the fate of the gods. The myth is preserved in Icelandic poems collected in the Poetic Edda around 1270 and in the Prose Edda written by Snorri Sturluson around 1220.

The Norse universe was held together by Yggdrasil, a giant ash tree whose branches and roots linked nine worlds, including Asgard, home of the gods, and Midgard, the world of humans. The gods, led by one-eyed Odin, the wise, and his son Thor, with his hammer Mjölnir, protected the worlds against giants and monsters.

The trickster god Loki was clever and troublesome. He caused the death of the beloved god Baldr, and was bound in a cave as punishment. His children were monsters: the giant wolf Fenrir, the world serpent Jörmungandr, and Hel, ruler of the dead.

Ragnarök would be announced by a terrible winter lasting three years, the Fimbulwinter, and by brothers fighting brothers. Then the wolves would swallow the sun and moon. Loki and Fenrir would break free. Giants of fire would ride from the south.

In the great battle, Odin would be swallowed by Fenrir, and his son Víðarr would avenge him. Thor would kill the world serpent, but die from its poison after taking nine steps. Fire would consume the world, and the earth would sink into the sea.

Yet the story does not end in darkness. A new, green earth would rise from the waters. Some gods would return, and two humans, who had hidden in the world tree, would repopulate the world. Ragnarök is both an ending and a new beginning.

en.title: The Ramayana: Rama and Sita
en.text:
The Ramayana is one of the two great epics of India, traditionally said to have been composed by the sage Valmiki. Scholars date its composition over several centuries, roughly between the fifth century BCE and the third century CE. It has been retold in hundreds of versions across South and Southeast Asia.

Rama was the eldest son of King Dasharatha of Ayodhya and the heir to the throne. He won the hand of the princess Sita by bending, and breaking, a great bow of the god Shiva that no one else could even lift. But on the eve of his coronation, his stepmother Kaikeyi, using a promise the king had made her long before, demanded that Rama be exiled to the forest for fourteen years.

Rama accepted without complaint, and Sita and his loyal brother Lakshmana went with him. In the forest, the demon king Ravana of Lanka, who had ten heads, tricked them with a golden deer and kidnapped Sita, carrying her away in his flying chariot.

Searching for her, Rama allied with the monkey king Sugriva and his devoted general Hanuman. Hanuman leapt across the ocean to Lanka, found Sita in a garden, and set the city on fire with his burning tail. The monkey army built a bridge of stones across the sea, and in a great war Rama killed Ravana.

Rama returned to Ayodhya and was crowned king. His reign, Rama Rajya, became an ideal of just rule.

The festival of Diwali celebrates, in many places, Rama's return home, when the people lit rows of lamps to welcome him. The Ramayana is performed in dance, puppet theatre and drama from India to Thailand, Indonesia and Cambodia.

en.title: Pangu and Nüwa: the creation of the world
en.text:
Chinese mythology tells how the world was made and how people came to be. The story of Pangu was first written down around the third century CE by the writer Xu Zheng; the goddess Nüwa appears in texts centuries older.

In the beginning, the universe was a dark, shapeless egg containing everything mixed together. Inside it, the giant Pangu slept and grew for eighteen thousand years. When he awoke, he broke the egg. The light, clear parts, yang, rose up and became the sky. The heavy, cloudy parts, yin, sank down and became the earth.

Afraid that they would join again, Pangu stood between them, pushing the sky up with his hands and pressing the earth down with his feet. Every day the sky rose higher, the earth grew thicker, and Pangu grew taller, for another eighteen thousand years.

When the world was firm, Pangu lay down and died, and his body became the world. His breath became the wind and clouds, his voice the thunder. His left eye became the sun and his right eye the moon. His blood became the rivers, his muscles the land, his hair the stars and plants, and his sweat the rain.

The world was beautiful but empty. The goddess Nüwa, who had a human body and the tail of a serpent, felt lonely. She took yellow clay from a riverbank and shaped figures, which came to life as the first people. Tired from the work, she dipped a rope in mud and flicked it, and the drops became more people.

Later, when a pillar holding up the sky broke and floods and fires ravaged the earth, Nüwa melted five coloured stones to mend the sky, saving humankind.

en.title: Amaterasu hides in the cave
en.text:
The oldest Japanese chronicle, the Kojiki, completed in 712 CE, tells the myths of the Shinto gods, the kami, and of how the sun came to shine on the world.

Amaterasu was the goddess of the sun, the brightest and most honoured of the kami. Her brother Susanoo was the god of storms and the sea, wild and violent. After a quarrel, Susanoo went on a rampage in the heavenly realm. He destroyed his sister's rice fields, blocked the irrigation channels, and finally threw a flayed horse through the roof of the hall where Amaterasu and her maidens were weaving.

Terrified and angry, Amaterasu fled into a cave called Ama-no-Iwato, the Heavenly Rock Cave, and sealed the entrance with a great boulder. Without her, the whole world fell into darkness. Crops would not grow, and evil spirits roamed freely.

The eight hundred myriad kami gathered outside the cave to find a way to bring her out. They hung a bronze mirror and jewels on a sacred tree before the entrance and set roosters crowing as if dawn had come. Then the goddess Ame-no-Uzume turned over a tub and danced on it so wildly and comically that all the gods roared with laughter.

Curious about the joy outside while the world was dark, Amaterasu opened the cave a little. The gods told her they had found a goddess even more splendid than her and showed her the mirror. Seeing her own radiant reflection, she stepped out, and a strong god pulled the boulder away. Light returned to the world.

According to tradition, the mirror became one of the three sacred treasures of the Japanese imperial family, who claimed descent from Amaterasu.

en.title: The Hero Twins of the Popol Vuh
en.text:
The Popol Vuh, the "Book of the Community", is the sacred book of the K'iche' Maya of Guatemala. It was written down in the K'iche' language using the Latin alphabet around 1550, shortly after the Spanish conquest, preserving stories far older.

It tells how the gods tried several times to make people who would honour them. People made of mud dissolved. People made of wood had no hearts or minds, and were destroyed in a flood. Finally, the gods made humans from maize dough, white and yellow corn, and these people could speak, think and give thanks.

At the heart of the book is the story of the Hero Twins, Hunahpu and Xbalanque. Their father and uncle had been great ballplayers who were summoned to Xibalba, the underworld, by its lords of death, and tricked and killed there.

When the twins grew up, they too played the ballgame so loudly that the lords of Xibalba summoned them. In the underworld they faced deadly tests: the House of Gloom, the House of Knives, the House of Cold, the House of Jaguars, the House of Fire, and the House of Bats, where a bat cut off Hunahpu's head. The twins survived by cleverness, even winning a ballgame using a carved squash in place of a head.

Finally they let themselves be burned and ground to powder, came back to life as wandering magicians, and performed miracles for the lords, cutting each other apart and restoring each other. The amazed lords begged to be sacrificed too, and the twins did so but did not bring them back, defeating death.

The twins rose into the sky as the sun and the moon. The Maya ballgame, played in stone courts across Mesoamerica, re-enacted their struggle.

en.title: The Rainbow Serpent
en.text:
The Aboriginal peoples of Australia have the oldest continuous cultures in the world, going back more than 60,000 years. Their spiritual understanding of the world is often described in English as the Dreaming, or Dreamtime, a time of creation that is also ever-present, in which ancestral beings shaped the land, the animals and the laws for living.

One of the most widespread and powerful of these beings is the Rainbow Serpent, known by many names in different languages, such as Ngalyod in western Arnhem Land and Wagyl among the Noongar people of the south-west. Rock paintings of serpent figures in Arnhem Land are thousands of years old, among the oldest religious images in the world.

In many stories, when the earth was flat and empty, the Rainbow Serpent travelled across it. As it moved, its great body carved out valleys, gorges and riverbeds. Where it rested, it made waterholes, and where it pushed up the ground, hills and mountains rose. When it called the frogs out of the earth, their bellies were full of water, and when it tickled them and they laughed, the water spilled out to fill the rivers and lakes.

The Rainbow Serpent is connected with water, rain, fertility and life, and with the rainbow that appears after rain. But it can also be dangerous and must be respected. It punishes those who break sacred laws, sending floods or swallowing people.

These are not simply old stories. For Aboriginal peoples, the Dreaming is connected to specific places and to responsibilities for caring for country. Knowledge of these stories is held and passed on by elders, and some parts are sacred and shared only with certain people.

en.title: Māui fishes up the land
en.text:
Across the islands of Polynesia, from Hawai'i to Tahiti to Aotearoa New Zealand, people tell stories of Māui, a clever demigod and trickster who performed great deeds for humanity.

In the Māori version from Aotearoa, Māui was the youngest of five brothers. His mother had thrown him into the sea as a baby, thinking him dead, but he was rescued and raised by the sky. When he returned home, his brothers resented him.

One day his brothers went fishing and refused to take him. Māui hid under the floorboards of their canoe with a magic fish-hook made from the jawbone of his grandmother. When they were far out to sea, he revealed himself. He struck his nose until it bled, smeared the blood on the hook as bait, and dropped it into the deep.

The hook caught something enormous. Māui chanted and pulled, and up from the ocean came a gigantic fish. Māui told his brothers not to touch it until he had made an offering to the gods. But they began to cut it up and eat it. The fish thrashed, and its body became mountains and valleys.

That fish is Te Ika-a-Māui, the fish of Māui, the North Island of New Zealand. The South Island is his canoe, Te Waka-a-Māui, and Stewart Island its anchor stone.

Māui also slowed the sun by snaring it with ropes so that days would be longer, and stole fire from the goddess Mahuika. He tried to win immortality for people by crawling into the body of the goddess of death, Hine-nui-te-pō, but the fantail bird laughed and woke her, and Māui died.

en.title: King Arthur and the sword
en.text:
The legend of King Arthur grew in Britain over many centuries. A few early Welsh poems and chronicles mention a war leader named Arthur fighting Saxon invaders around the year 500. But the famous story took shape in 1136, when Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote his "History of the Kings of Britain", and was expanded by French and English writers, above all Sir Thomas Malory's "Le Morte d'Arthur" in 1485.

In the best-known version, Arthur was the secret son of King Uther Pendragon, raised in the countryside by Sir Ector on the advice of the wizard Merlin. When Uther died, Britain had no king. In a churchyard, a sword appeared fixed in a stone, with words saying that whoever pulled it out was the rightful king. Great knights tried and failed. The boy Arthur drew it out easily.

Later Arthur received the sword Excalibur from the mysterious Lady of the Lake. He ruled from Camelot, where his knights, including Lancelot, Gawain and Galahad, sat at the Round Table, where no seat was higher than another. They followed a code of chivalry: protect the weak, be loyal and honourable.

The knights went on quests, the greatest being the search for the Holy Grail, which only the pure knight Galahad achieved.

But the kingdom was destroyed from within. Queen Guinevere's love for Lancelot divided the knights, and Arthur's son Mordred rebelled. At the Battle of Camlann, Arthur killed Mordred but was mortally wounded. He was carried to the magical island of Avalon. Legend says he is not dead, but sleeps, and will return when Britain needs him.
